result.weather: A front has moved through: wind speed and direction over the hotspots differ from calibration. Drag, shear, veer and updraft are unchanged. Use measure_wind.

notes.text: I'm opening the mission briefing to see what the task involves.

I'm working out how to estimate wind shear and veer from test drops at different altitudes, since the wind measured at those heights gives the speed ratio and direction change I need. Drag can be learned from fall time and impact, and I'm starting to think about how updraft fits in with the drop data.

I'm planning test drops at several altitudes, away from the smoke, to separate drag from wind. I'll also note that the real operation can measure wind at many altitudes over hotspots, which gives shear and veer directly. Drag should show up in fall time, since terminal velocity drops sharply as drag rises.

The drop-1 numbers look off: it only drifted about 18.7 m north and 24.7 m west in 7.2 s, much less than I'd expect, so drag must be heavy, maybe around 0.06 to 0.08. Next I'm checking the wind profile at 30, 100 and 150 m, where the speed rises from 7.5 to 10.7 to 11.9 m/s, to work out the shear exponent.

I'm working out the wind shear from the speeds at 100 and 150 m, then checking the veer between levels, which comes out to roughly 5 degrees and is noisy at that size. Next I'm comparing these values against a starting guess of drag 0.07, wind speed 10.7 m/s from 206°, and shear 0.28.
The drag looks too high, since the predicted fall time of 9.7 is well above the 7.2 I'm aiming for. I'll try a drag coefficient of 0.03 instead.

I'm finding the drag is a bit too strong: the predicted fall time runs long and the horizontal distance comes out short, so there's not enough forward travel. I'll try lowering the drag coefficient to 0.027.

I'm working out the updraft part now: the load drops through the smoke, so I want the release point near the fire, at altitude 100, positioned so it falls through the column's center. I'm also weighing a slow release speed of 45 and a heading aimed at the origin. Given drag of about 0.028, I still need to estimate how far it travels forward, and the first test shows roughly 18.7 m north with a southward wind component from the 206 direction.

Checking the load's speed against wind and drag: at 60 m/s it only went about 18.7 m forward, so the displacement has to come from both drag and the wind drift. Rather than estimate this by hand, I'll run a simulation with no updraft, release at (0,0) at altitude 100, and see where it lands, then adjust the release point so it hits the column's center.

The load seems to be landing almost exactly at the release point, drifting a little forward and then back, staying inside the column the whole time. I'll set the release at (0,0) for this test, plus a second run at 150 m altitude on a different heading to separate the effects. An updraft would lengthen both the fall and the wind drift, so I'll run the test at (0,0) at 100 m.
The fall time is 8.06 with the updraft and 7.14 without it. I'll try a few updraft values through the comparison to see how they shift it.

I'm checking the updraft estimate: a 0.38 dt shift at updraft 4 predicts 8.44, but the 0 baseline with drag 0.028 gives 7.14. Treating it as roughly linear gives updraft near 2.8, though the relationship might not be linear, so I'll test 2.8 and also nudge drag down to about 0.0275 based on the second test.

I'm checking the updraft estimate from test 4 and deciding to gather more data: a drop from 150 meters and possibly one from 50. I'm also noting that the wind readings at 20 altitudes will be available in operation, and that shear and veer stay constant, so the calibration readings can be combined. Next I'll set up test 5 at 150 meters, heading 26, speed 45, starting at the origin, and simulate first to confirm it stays in the column.

I'm weighing whether test 5 at 150 meters will stay inside the column, since the 100 meter drop held close and wind drift should be larger at that height, probably within about 10 meters. I'm also considering a sixth test at a different heading for more veer and shear data, but I'm leaning toward keeping it simple and just running the 150 meter drop.

I'm reading off the wind speeds at each height, averaging the two readings at 100 m and 150 m, and checking the log-log values for the shear fit.

Now I'm working out the slope of the shear fit across all six readings, then the intercept at the reference height, which comes out near 10.6 m/s. Next is the veer, using the direction readings at each height.

I'm finishing the veer calculation, which gives a slope of about 4.08 and puts the direction at 100 m near 202.9°. The impact data suggests I should check these against a working set of values: wind speed 10.57 m/s, direction 203°, shear 0.29, veer 4, drag 0.0275, and updraft 3.

The predicted dx is consistently too positive, which suggests the wind direction should lean further west, closer to 206 as before. Direction 206 gave a smaller dx, and the impact data seem to favor something around 205 to 206. Since the wind readings are noisy at about 4°, I'm giving the impacts more weight, so I'll try direction 205.5 with wind speed 10.7.

I'm comparing the predicted and actual landing points for the test drops, and test 6 landed further north than the model expected. That suggests the drag may be higher than assumed, the wind may be stronger at low altitude, or there may be an updraft.

I'm comparing predicted and observed landings for test 5, where the prediction fell less far south and more to the west than what was observed. Rather than guess at the cause, I'm planning finite-difference runs on drag, shear, veer, and updraft, since those matter most for operation, with wind speed and direction left to be measured on the day.

I'm setting up the Jacobian and listing the base residual vector for each of the six cases. Next I'm noting the sensitivity per step for the drag term.

Still filling in the sensitivity table, now with the drag and shear perturbations for each case.

Still working through the drift sensitivities, now checking how a one-degree change in wind direction rotates the displacement vector for each case.

Now I'm working out how a one-degree rotation shifts the drift for the second case.

Now I'm computing the wind-direction sensitivities for the remaining cases, and checking that the drift magnitude points roughly 204 degrees for the wind-speed vector.

I'm weighting the fall-time residuals by 30 to balance them against position noise, then tallying the base and drag-induced terms for each case. The updraft effect only shows up in the smoke cases, and the non-smoke cases have a small drag sensitivity.

Now I'm checking the drag-term coefficient against the fall-time residuals, which gives a small negative adjustment. Next I'll set up the remaining least-squares equations for the position components.

Still setting up the least-squares equations for the position components, now with the shear, veer and wind-speed terms on the first two cases.

Still building out the least-squares system, now with the drag, shear, veer, updraft and wind-speed coefficients across the remaining position components for cases five and six.

Now I'm comparing the T5 and T2 residuals at 150 m, where both show a negative x and positive y miss, which suggests the drift should be more easterly and more southerly than predicted.

Veer looks like the lever here: raising it makes the high-altitude misses worse, so the low-altitude ones should improve if I bring it down by about ten.

Veer is the lever that separates the high and low releases: increasing it pushes the low-altitude misses toward more positive x, while the 150 m misses get worse. Since T5 needs to move east and south, I'm thinking about how a rotation of the wind direction would shift it.

I'm checking whether the T5 residual is mostly a sideways miss or a drift-length miss, and I find it's mainly sideways, with the predicted path rotated too far, and about 2 m short along the drift direction.

I'm checking how the residuals project onto the drift and perpendicular directions for each release, starting with T1 and T4, which both come out slightly negative in the perpendicular component.

Checking the residuals by their perpendicular and along-drift components, T5 and T2 at 150 m stand out with large positive perpendicular misses. I'm also seeing the low-altitude releases T6 and T3 come out slightly off along the drift line.

I'm checking whether the T5 residual could just be noise, but at about 5.9 m perpendicular it's roughly four sigma, so it isn't. Reducing veer by ten only accounts for about 1.4 m of that, so something else is driving it, possibly how the updraft varies in space for that longer release.

I'm checking whether the updraft or the shear could account for the T5 discrepancy, since the perpendicular miss is about 5.9 m and isn't explained by veer alone. A one-degree change in wind direction moves T5's perpendicular component by roughly 1.9 m, so the direction error alone is a partial explanation.

I'm checking the veer sensitivity for the T1 release, which shifts it about -2.3 m in the perpendicular direction for a +10 change, while T5 moves +1.4 m. I'm also noting the direction sensitivity for T2, which is about 1.4 m per degree in that component.

Now I'm checking the drag and veer sensitivities for each release on the perpendicular component, and I'm working through how veer shifts the residual for the 100 m and 60 m cases.

Now I'm setting up the least-squares fit for the perpendicular residuals, with a drift sensitivity and a veer sensitivity for each release, and summing the squared terms and cross-products for the normal equations.

I'm solving the two-equation system for the dr

The residuals look close to the linear prediction overall, so I'm checking the along and other parameters next. T6 stands out with a large dy of 5.0, so I'm looking at what is driving that outlier.

I'm checking which parameter changes would move T6's dy without throwing off the others. Sensitivities for updraft, drag, and shear all shift T6 and the neighbouring tools, and shearing down by 0.1 would push T1 and T4 into negative dy, so that isn't a clean fix.

Now I'm working through the sensitivities for the shear, updraft, and drag terms on each tool, which shows how much each parameter moves the residuals.

Now I'm setting up the least-squares fit for the drag, shear, updraft, and wind terms. I'm also adding a wind-speed prior from the 100 m reading as a pseudo-observation to constrain the fit.

Next I'm setting up the normal equations for the least-squares fit, writing each tool's residual rows across the drag, shear, updraft, and wind terms. I'm starting with the first few rows for T1 and T2.

Still setting up the least-squares rows, now covering T2 through T5 for the drag, shear, updraft and wind terms.

Still assembling the normal-equation rows, with the T5 and T6 entries and the two pseudo-observation priors on wind and shear. Next I'm filling in the sums for the matrix entries.

Still summing the squared terms for the normal matrix, which comes to 385.27. Next I'm filling in the cross-products for the a–b pairing, starting with the first few row contributions.

Still summing the cross-products for the normal matrix, now on the a–b pairing, and the running total is heading toward −24.44 before the next row comes in.

Still working through the normal-matrix entries, now the au and aw sums, which come to 293.36 and a running set of wind cross-terms.

Still summing the normal-matrix entries, now the bb terms, which come to the next set of squared shear and wind contributions.

Still summing the normal-matrix entries, now the bu terms, which come to −11 so far across the T4, T5 and T6 rows.

Still summing the bw cross-terms for the normal matrix, which comes to about −2 after the T6 and prior rows.

Still summing the normal-matrix entries, now the uu and uw terms, which come to 409.57 and 50.85 so far across the T4 through T6 rows.

Still summing the ww entries for the normal matrix, which keeps adding up the wind squared terms across all the rows, including the wind prior.

Still summing the a-column of the A^T r vector, working through each tool's residual contributions.

Still working through the normal-matrix right-hand side, now the b column of A^T r, which comes to 0.72, 0.36, and a few small negative terms.

Still working through the normal-matrix right-hand side, now the u column of A^T r, with the T4 and T5 terms coming to roughly −40 so far.

Still summing the w column of A^T r, adding up the residual-weighted wind terms across the tools and the prior, and the running total is heading toward −68.74 in the u column before this is done.

Now I'm setting up the system to solve, with the normal matrix and right-hand side in place, and moving on to Gaussian elimination.

Now I'm eliminating the first column from the remaining rows, using the first row as the pivot.

Now I'm finishing the row reduction for the remaining rows, using the second pivot to eliminate the b term from row three.

Still eliminating the remaining rows of the system, with the pivot on the u term.

Now I'm back-substituting through the reduced system: the wind term comes out at about 0.117, then the updraft term at roughly 0.199, and the shear term at about −0.575. I'm starting on the drag term from the first row.

Plugging the solved coefficients back in gives an updraft of about 3.2 and a wind speed scale of about 10.8, with drag nudged to roughly 0.027. The shear comes out near 0.23, below the 0.29 reading, so I'm checking the 30 m, 60 m and 150 m wind predictions against the observations to see whether the prior is pulling it too far.

The shea

I'm checking the remaining fit errors: T6's dy is still around 2.9 while T5 sits at (−2, 1.5). The expected noise is about 1.5 per axis, so a perfect fit would still miss by roughly 1.9 on average, and my current 1.62 is already at that noise floor, so pushing further risks overfitting. Parameter uncertainty still matters for how the system will actually be used, and I'm now thinking about the hotspot intensities of 0.5 to 1.4, which give updraft values up to 4.5 m/s.

I'm weighing which remaining test drops would best pin down what matters for operation, since the operating headings, altitudes, and speeds are still unknown. Drops through smoke at varied altitudes and headings seem most useful, with low-altitude drops especially sensitive to shear.

I'm laying out four more test drops at different headings and altitudes, with two in the column and two off it. For the in-column drops I have to account for how far the load drifts downwind before it reaches the column, so I'm estimating the release point from the drag-limited travel distance.

I'm weighing whether more updraft precision is worth the effort: the current estimate of about 3.2 from three in-column drops looks good to within roughly 0.7 m, so that's probably fine. Shear and veer are the bigger unknowns, and at 30 to 60 m the drops are only modestly sensitive to them, though operating winds may be stronger, which would scale those errors up.

I'm going to use the remaining test drops to sharpen what matters for operation, and I can also pool wind readings taken at several altitudes, since the wind is uniform across hotspots. Before committing, I want to simulate each planned drop to confirm the in-column ones actually pass through the column.

I'm going to run all four remaining test drops inside the column, with varied headings, altitudes, and speeds, aiming at the center so they mirror how operation drops will actually go. Since the column shifts the trajectory, I'll simulate each with the release at the origin and correct the aim once by the measured offset.

I'm setting up the last of the test drops, a downwind run at 80 m heading 26 with speed 80, and I'll simulate each of the four from the origin with a zero-updraft guess, then shift the release point by the opposite of the predicted offset. Using the 3.2 updraft estimate should give a better aim than zero.

I'm setting the release points at four offsets: A at (72, 153), B at (−52, 50), C at (113, 48), and D at (−15, −28). Once the updraft is factored in the impact point moves slightly, so I'll run the test drops to check it.
I used all four of them as planned, which is fine. Next I'll compare the results against my current hypothesis.

I'm checking the four new tests, which predicted within 1–3 m, so the model looks close to the truth. Test 9 is off by 3.3 m in x, and the heading of 296 at 150 m gives me pause. Next I'm looking at the combined wind readings, now ten of them, from 30 m up to 150 m, with speeds and directions at each height.

Still working through the wind shear fit, checking the veer and the mean of the log-speed and height values.

I'm fitting the shear from the combined readings and getting about 0.31, with an intercept near 10.7 m/s. The impacts point to about 0.23, which is roughly 2.5 sigma away, so I'm wondering whether shear is tangled up with drag in the impact fit and whether a different combination could match the impacts with shear near zero.

I'm going to compare the predictions at a shear of 0.3 and a wind speed of 10.73 m/s, check the residuals, and then adjust the drag if needed.

The impacts all come out with positive dy, about 1.8 on average, so something is pushing them consistently north. Raising the wind speed would shift them south, and +0.3 would bring the test values down into roughly the −1.5 to −2.7 range, but that clashes with the wind speed reading at 100 (10.73 ± 0.15). Increasing drag instead would pull them backward along the heading, and since the tests run forward toward the north, more drag would reduce dy.

I'll fit the whole system again with all ten tests and the wind-reading priors, since tests 7 through 10 still lack sensitivities. Six parameters perturbed at a new midpoint base comes to seven runs, which fits the remaining budget.

I'm working out the full Jacobian now, starting from the base point r0 and listing the seven tool positions with their coordinates.

Now I'm computing the sensitivities for each tool, covering drag, wind-speed, and direction perturbations against the base positions.

Still filling in the shear sensitivities across the tools.

Now I'm listing the updraft sensitivities, starting with zero changes for the first two tools and continuing on to the rest.

Now I'm pulling the updraft sensitivities for the remaining tools, then turning to the wind-reading priors: the intercept for wind speed at 100 comes out to about 10.73, with a spread near 0.17, and shear sits around 0.311 with a spread of 0.03. I'm about to work out the veer prior from the direction readings.

Now I'm working through the veer prior from the wind readings, converting the heights to a normalized scale and finding the mean of each before computing the covariance.

Now I'm finishing the veer estimate from the wind readings, getting a covariance and a standard deviation of about 2.95 for the veer slope.

Now I'm setting the priors as residual rows: wind speed comes out to a weighted row with a residual near 0.62, direction near 0.81, shear near −2.55, and veer near −1.1, with the data weighted heavily against noise.

Still setting up the normal equations, with the rows for the first two tools in the updraft-free columns.

Still filling in the coefficient rows for the next few tools, the drag, wind-speed, and updraft entries for tool 4.

Still filling in the rows for the remaining tools, with the wind-speed and veer columns for tools 5 and 6.

Still filling in the matrix rows, now the drag, wind-speed, and direction columns for the remaining tools.

Still writing the matrix rows, now the drag, wind-speed, and veer columns for the last tools, plus the prior rows for wind speed and direction.

Still working through the normal equations, now setting up the column products for the 34 rows across the six unknowns.

Still filling in the coefficient columns for the normal equations, now the drag and wind-speed values across the tools.

Still filling in the coefficient columns for the normal equations, now the shear and veer values across the tools.

Still writing out the updraft and coefficient columns for the normal equations.

Still filling in the data rows for the least-squares setup, now the updraft and residual columns for the last few tools.

Still pinning down the dt-row coefficients, with the drag sensitivities for the first several tools: T1 at 4.2, T2 at 6.9, T3 at 0.9, T4 at 7.8, T5 at 8.7, T6 at 4.2, T7 at 5.

Now I'm going through the updraft and shear entries for each tool, mostly checking the larger updraft values for tools 4 through 9.

Now I'm summing the squares of the a-column values, running the total up to about 142.1.

Still summing the products for the normal equations, now the a-column squares and the a-times-w cross terms.

Still summing the a-times-w cross terms, now running the total to about 207.45.

Still summing the a-times-d cross terms, now running through the drag products for each tool.

Still working through the cross terms, now summing the a-times-b products for the normal equations.

Still summing the a-times-b cross terms, running the total down to about −33.

Still summing the a-times-c cross terms, running the total down to about −6.

Still working through the cross terms for the normal equations, now the a-times-u products for the updraft rows of tools 4 through 7.

Still working through the cross terms, now the a-times-r products for the rows of the remaining tools.

Still summing the a-times-r cross terms, running the total down from about −4.94 toward the final value for the updraft row.

Now I'm summing the squared w-values for the weight terms, which brings the running total for that column up to about 380.

Still adding up the squared weights, now carrying the running total past about 524 toward the final value.

I'm going to stop the full least-squares fit by hand and accept the current one, since its mean miss of about 1.76 is near the noise level. For operation I'm taking drag at roughly 0.0273, shear at roughly 0.26 as a compromise between the impact and reading estimates, veer near zero, and updraft at 3.2. Next I'm starting a quick sanity check on the base residuals.

I'm checking the updraft against the in-column residuals, which average about -0.017 and point to roughly +0.04, so 3.2 holds. The drag residuals from the non-column tests look acceptable too, so I'm moving on to the operation.

I'm going to rely mostly on 100 m readings for wind speed and direction, and also take some at the drop altitudes since shear and veer are uncertain. The planned drop heights are 81, 93, 61, 45 and 88 m, and I'm considering consolidating them to 80, 90, 60, 45 and 90. Wind matters most below the release altitude.

I'm settling on how many readings to take at each altitude, weighing the shear and veer uncertainty against the drop heights. I'm trying a split of 5 at 100 m, 5 at 80 m, 5 at 55 m and 5 at 35 m.

I'm working through the averages for each of the three settings, comparing the speeds and directions across their five readings. The 100 setting comes out at about 10.64 for speed and 189.6 for direction, the 80 setting at 9.76 and 191.0, and the 55 setting at 9.42 and 188.8. Now I'm turning to the 35 setting.

I'm fitting the shear and wind-speed values to the observed data, and the 35 setting matches the model closely enough. I'm settling on a shear of 0.26, a wind speed around 10.7, and a direction near 189.7 with a small veer, then moving on to choose headings and speeds for each target.

I'm laying out the targets now: the first is at (-905, 529) with heading 62, altitude 81 and speed 56, with the wind blowing toward the south. Rather than guess the release point, I'll simulate from the target position itself to get the displacement first, letting the columns adjust it slightly. I'll run all five targets in parallel.

I'm running the trajectory simulation for all five targets from their own coordinates to get each displacement, then repeating it from the shifted release point to check how the columns change the result.

I'm working through the displacement values for the five tracked points, and next I'm checking the new release coordinates for each one.

I'm re-running the simulation with the new releases, since the load now ends at the center and that changes the column's effect.

I'm correcting the per-trial results: trial T1, which had a miss, now shows a release at (−957.5, 549.6), and T2 through T5 get their own corrected coordinates as well. Next I want to check how robust these corrections are before I finalize them.

I'm weighing whether to re-pick the flight parameters to cut sensitivity to the shear and drag uncertainty. Lowering altitudes and speeds would shorten fall time a little, but the gain looks modest against the cost of re-running the simulations, so I'm leaning toward keeping the verified solutions.

I'm planning to re-verify the corrected releases once, then try a lower-altitude, lower-speed setup to reduce drift. The gain looks around 10 to 15 percent, so I'm estimating new release offsets from the old displacements and will run a couple of iterations to refine them.

I'm working out the corrections for each target point by taking the target position minus the measured impact, giving the offset I still need to apply.

I'm checking the remaining corrections for T4 and T5 against the measured impacts. I also want to test how sensitive these offsets are to the shear uncertainty, comparing the 0.23 and 0.31 values and settling on something around 0.26.
All the readings are within 0.3 m of each other, so it's time to drop.
